en: 4. The Section on the Duration of the States of Happiness and Suffering within the State of Evolution.
4.3. The Account of Internal Dissolution: There are three fires of dissolution known as famine, disease, and weapons.
As if now emitting smoke, they are about to blaze forth at the end of the future eon.
This world, moreover, fans those fires for its own destruction with the favorable fuel of envy, evil, and anger.
Excessive rain, drought, and unseasonable rains,
accompanied by portents, increase terrible famine like a poisonous tree.
Indeed, this dissolution shall occur specifically through famine.
But his sickness and weapons will be like attendants;
in this world plagued by famine, food and drink will be exceedingly difficult to find,
yet for some great beings here and there, it will exist like the true Dharma.
Having seized and even killed embodied beings, they will provide for their livelihood;
indeed, the predominance of unrighteousness arises for the sake of mutual destruction.
Thus, even without obtaining food from kingdoms, villages, or families—

Like lotuses drained of water, they will gradually go to ruin. Then, because of their engagement in unrighteousness, the seasons, as if displeased, will have irregular courses and will spoil their food.
Afflicted by food that has entered their bodies like a ripening sin,
they shall go toward various diseases accompanied by *piśāca* demons.
Driven by manifold illnesses and *piśāca*s, they will seek relief.
"By performing sacrifices characterized by violence, they will increase calamities;
thus, here in this world, there will be a gradual decline of the districts, villages, and families who are afflicted by disease, like that of lotuses pained by frost. [4.3.10–11]
Then, for those who crave enjoyments and harbor mutual malice toward one another,
a great weapon shall arise like the cresting flames of the fire of their anger. The lords of men from the east, the north, the west, and the south— [4.3.12] — [shall rise up].
The winds seem as if they will rush against one another for the sake of mutual destruction;
[4.3.13] and kings, having provoked one another into agitation, will repeatedly rise and break apart like waves upon the ocean. [4.3.14]

These people, with fires of anger arising from the fuel of greed, burning one another, will bring about the destruction of their own families. As for the remaining families in these villages of sense-objects, they too will [destroy] one another here.

Embracing one another while burning with the fire of anger, they will perish like forest timber. [4.3.16] With blades of grass and other things arising from their own evil deeds that feel like weapons to the touch, even two or three of them will slay each other, like those on the side of unwholesome conduct. [4.3.17]

Driven to the end of three destructions, mortals will have a lifespan of ten years; deprived of beauty, stature, and strength, they will remain for seventy years. For these seven times sevenfold miserable beings, the years, months, and days [will be likewise diminished].
In groups of three, two, or one, they shall perish by means of famine, disease, and arrows.
Devoted solely to evil, this world of humans will for the most part go to the lowest states of woe.
For having followed the downward slope of the dark abyss— the path of evil—
who that is devoid of effort would not sink lower than this? Thus,
for human beings, the three cycles of destruction arrive.
Like trees that have encountered a forest fire,
some mortal here or there, through the quality of separation from others,
became exceedingly moist with a mind of loving-kindness, like a tree. [4.3.21]
Seeing that even among the remaining mortals there were some who had not abandoned the path of the virtuous despite the onset of evil,
she thought, "May this [corruption] not cut through the people."
The lords of the yakṣas became their protectors;
having approached them with a mind full of compassion, they departed after the remainder of the eon had passed through its hardships.
For when there is a lapse in ritual action, sins find their opportunity and are not able to coexist with merit.
This concludes the third rest, titled "The Account of the Intermediate Dissolution," in the fourth section.
4.4. The Account of the Eleven Kalpas:
"Then, having seen one another, mortals will embrace each other with joy like friends; the tenth kalpa will come to pass as it brings them together. [4.4.1]

They shall proceed by the auspicious path like the planets and the remaining mortals; they shall become free from defects like the seasons under the guidance of a sage. When external and internal phenomena have thus attained a state of equality, [4.4.2]
There shall be sovereignty over the Dharma and unimpeded happiness.
There will be other mortals born there, as well as embodied beings born from them and born from those;
they shall have a lifespan of twenty thousand years, and their lifespans shall double and double again.

In the houses of those men who possess preeminent excellence, a maiden of five hundred years shall be given as a bride, like the goddess Lakṣmī herself flourishing there. Their beauty and other physical perfections will be in accordance with their lifespan.
What desired merit would it not attract, which faces every direction?
[4.4.6] The world, filled with villages situated on the advice of the "Cock's Crowing," will possess abundant splendor, like the sky with its stars. [4.4.7]
Like a multitude of people seeking absolute purity, the earth will descend,
having cast down all impurities as if they were sins;
when the side of happiness arises, it sinks down into its own side.
He will meet his death in misery, for the rise of an enemy is indeed hard to endure.
Delighted by the very happiness that accompanies all their prosperity,
people will not even remember our suffering when we are away from home.
"Having cast aside the mere exhaustion caused by cold, heat, hunger, thirst, old age, and desire—
[exhaustion] which belongs only to the worldly person who deals with suffering—
[they] shall not allow their lives to reach the great excellence attained in immeasurable autumns. [4.4.11] Thus they shall proceed.

For a state of single-minded devotion to the Dharma does not allow for the opportunity of decline. However, having reached the stage of ten or eleven [qualities], they may at some point lose them again; for even prosperities, though they endure for a long time, end in misfortune.

Having fallen away from the Dharma, they have reached the state of being ten years of age; they will demonstrate the downward path for those falling from the heights to the depths. Thus, when the world has come to this state, the eon will reach its tenth stage.
Let it be that this is not pleasant to hear; something else is now being stated:
"Just as this tenth aeon is joined with pleasure and pain, so too will ten others exist in the future, following after it. [4.4.15]
In this world, these phenomena that come into being even without a conscious mind generally follow the patterns of the past;
thus, this world-system remains as it has evolved.
From sunrise for twenty kalpas,
having removed as it were the fatigue of so much rising,
he will depart from above like one terrified of universal dissolution.
The Fourth Resting Place, titled "The Account of the Eleven Kalpas."
And the fourth [section] is the chapter on the persistence of pleasure and pain during the state of evolution.
5. The Section on the State of Dissolution 5.1. The Dissolution of Sentient Beings:
When the remaining population has dissolved, [they attain] supreme loving-kindness.
Having done so, he sends word to one another by means of a vision:
"From this I understand that even in this world, men obtain a fruit corresponding to their mental disposition. [5.1.1]
Then, another kalpa, pleasant in its beginning, middle, and end, will arrive, delightful in its festival of loving-kindness;
for this very reason, they shall assume a beautiful attire.
All external things and those other than them are like a third story of an exalted mansion, through the auspicious succession of steps as it were. [5.1.2]
Having ascended to this state consisting of loving-kindness, the world shall experience its splendor until the dissolution of all things;
through that supreme loving-kindness, beings will emerge into manifestation.
By a stroke of fortune, even those who have fallen into the three miserable realms maintain a state of moistened compassion toward suffering beings under the guise of loving-kindness; thus,
the Ordainer has ordained a compassionate equanimity as the very nature of Dharma.
"Both these people and we ourselves have been brought to this miserable state by our own actions; why then are we angry with others?
Having thought thus, both the victims and the executioners should cultivate loving-kindness.
For they will go from the lower hells to another realm hereafter;
thus, even in one or another of the lower states of woe,
having approached loving-kindness as if it were a great accomplishment.
Having destroyed the evil that constitutes its opposite, they shall attain hereafter, among men and gods, those very peaceful states just like the perfected ones. [5.1.6]
Having vacated his dwellings and departed from this world, and having established the remaining people in the state of the Sugata,
Dharma himself will exercise supreme sovereignty.
Then the multitudes of men who proclaim [it], the assemblies of heretics,
and the gods belonging to the Ābhāsvara class of deities—
like the officials of a sovereign of the Dharma— they [follow] what has been set forth by him.
At that time, they explain the principle that is beyond discursive thought:
"In former times, humans with a lifespan of ten thousand years encountered bondage and slaughter amidst sensual desires."
Having heard this from them and having become disgusted with sensual desires,
people will attain the second dhyāna,
which is free from all defects such as desire.
Possessing clarity, bound by joy and bliss, and assuming the grace of a staircase for the sake of attaining the Ābhāsvara realm, that will come to be for them. [5.1.10]
Having produced other meditative concentrations even from that stage, they will go back to that very same body,
for it is by means of an internal conforming [path] as well.
They attain the stage that is accessible by way of the root-path; thus,
as these people pass away,
they [go] to the Ābhāsvara [heaven].
Having given away this earth, which is like a borrowed ornament for the world of men, it will no longer shine;
having cast aside the eight celestial bodies below.
Even the gods will go to that assembly,
leaving behind their inferior state to attain excellence,
where the wise eternally triumph. [5.1.13]
This dissolution of living beings has begun;
having reached Brahmā, it shall come to an end.
He alone [remains] for this world of the moving and the unmoving.

[5.1.14] While the world is becoming void, even the other ten kalpas, which were capable of perceiving it when it possessed a beginning and an end, have been turned back by this alone, being rendered powerless even to look upon it.
This thousandfold world-system, as if overcome by extreme fainting,
does not perceive the suffering born of separation from its people.
In the fifth book, the first rest-period, titled "The Dissolution of Beings," concludes.
Thus, at that time, while this world was empty,
the god did not rain for an exceedingly long period.
Deprived of their milk, these calves— representing the clusters of creepers, grasses, and trees— wither away.
Like one parched with thirst and desiring to drink from rivers flowing through rugged ravines, [he seeks relief].
A second sun, twice as great, shall arise here;
overwhelmed by that which has appeared from the third heaven, the hosts of gods below in the sky shall suffer. [5.2.2]
From this [lake], the third [lake] below it, which measures double its size, is heated;
at that time, the lakes undergo desiccation as if out of fear of being drunk.
Even the unfathomable lakes, such as Mānasa and others, will dry up. The fourth sun, Vivasvat, twice as large as the third,
scorching from below, hangs suspended from the Tuṣita heaven.
For whom the seven rivers will cease their burning from the mere falling of a handful of water;
by means of the fourth [vowel], the two-mora [vowel] is able to burn only that which is below.
Vivasvat, who will hereafter delight in emanations,
seeing him as one parched with thirst for the stream of the Dharma,
shall enter this lovely-bodied one who has no other protector. [5.2.5]
Even as it flows gradually toward the lower ground, the lord of rivers will eventually reach a level surface;
this is truly what those whose nature is water declare.
Actions have perverted fruits.
[5.2.6] Without a mind possessing deep momentum,
having reached exhaustion through being solely intent on agitation, it withers away.
Having placed impermanence as if in the palm of his hand,
he will demonstrate it to those who are exceedingly difficult to subdue;
for even today, the mountains are submerged in that ocean.
If even those who are unable to emerge from the water with their heads held high are subject to such a state,
what then will certainly become of other beings born in the refined world? [5.2.8]
Having drunk this today, they will surely carry us away like clouds borne by the wind;
there shall not remain even a space the size of a finger-joint.
What could there be here that offers consolation,
when even the king of waters— who is not led by others, who is steadfast in his own nature, and who goes to destruction— [must perish]? [5.2.9]
There is no conditioned thing whatsoever that is non-perishable;
therefore, this doctrine regarding it is utterly false.
Even by the winds of cosmic dissolution, it cannot today be shattered.
The ocean, which can be fathomed by virtue of its depth, might be said to perish upon being breached; but who are those refined persons who, like me, are not themselves fragile? [5.2.11]
Just as the lord of the waters, though possessing no other enjoyment, undergoes old age and destruction within his own body,
so too is it with whatever is conditioned that exists right there.
Therefore, that shattered protection is of no use at all.
Having robbed it of its mountain-like beauty, the timiṅgilas and other sea-monsters now sport upon it without any regard, having taken refuge there.
When that ocean has perished, what other conditioned thing could there be for dissolution, or what refuge could there be?
Therefore, one is able to find relief from the flood of existence.
Like a house blazing on all sides,
who that is wise would find delight in this, where there is not even the slightest merit or fault? [5.2.14]
It is sufficient to be completely detached from all existence;
passion is not beneficial when directed toward this [world]. For who would have a desire for food mixed with poison?
He brings peace, not indeed destruction.
Possessing double power, the sun of sovereign control, about to burn that which stands below from the fifth [station], will prevail.
Then, as if exhausted, the serpents and other creatures dwelling within the earth will emit smoke and sighs in every direction;
for they are situated directly beneath everything above, in order to burn it.

From the sixth [Manu], Vivasvat will be of two morae; he alone will be capable of burning away all desires. Thus, the Creator showed indifference toward him for the sake of creating another world. [5.2.17]
In this thousandfold world-system, there are this many celestial palaces belonging to the king of gods, each supported from above by seven suns;
having eclipsed the rows of parasols over the multitudes of the Sugata’s reliquaries, they stand there.
They will depart as if full of regret and intense remorse.
[5.2.18] This concludes the second rest-period in the fifth section, titled "The Rising of the Sun."
5.3. The Dissolution of the Elements: The entire world, mounted upon the funeral pyre of instability, is enveloped in smoke by the primordial suns.

Even the final rites of the great are illuminated by the light of the great for those who long for liberation; then, with uplifted flames and a roar as terrifying as a hundred [thunderclaps], [he appeared]. [5.3.1] Athoddhatārciḥ śatabhīmanādo.
Like a fire about to consume the earth, impermanence and I shall devour everything; therefore, do not be heedless here regarding anything at all. [5.3.2]
Having passed the time with the play of the waters, even the Lord of Waters, though he is to be consumed by the fire at the end of an eon, [remains];
truly, there is no such thing as wealth that is eternal.
Surely those who follow after misfortune do not escape it:
Mount Meru, about to be consumed by fire, will be struck by its peaks as they fall with a loud roar.
"Who would not fall into misfortune like an intoxicated man from a very high place?"—thus it seems to say.
"Like a bronze vessel containing but little water. [5.3.4]
Heated, she drinks the ocean beneath the earth;
she will find no satisfaction until his drinking-vessel has been drained entirely.
Having thus swallowed his own support— the receptacle world— just as one might swallow human ashes and the like,
he will perish like one who eats his own flesh.
Having become supportless like the fire at the end of an eon, six suns— each rising with its own additional light— having scorched the world individually for one and a half kalpas, [5.3.6]...
As if thinking, "Let not even my final eon be consumed by more than that," everything blazed up at the very moment of being fanned.
Those suns, having caused intense torment to the world, shall perish along with the universe; indeed,
they do not meet their destruction immediately.
Thinking, "Having been created as consisting of fire,
she might burn everything and perhaps even come near me," [he remained] as if in that state of the world.
The Creator approaches the summit of the world-destruction;
even the hosts of those who dwell in the abodes of the Ordainer shall depart to those regions that are unstruck by time.
"For where the Lord himself has no power to remain,
there the talk of others has already departed.
Thus was the root *sah* [explained] by the Fire-god.
Everything would be non-existent, just as it is not;
for all things possess an identical nature at the prior limit, just as they do in their state of being situated in the middle. [5.3.11]
Therein, twenty eons pass, arising and dissolving simultaneously;
having become like a vast abyss, who is capable of transcending destruction?
The third rest in the fifth section, titled "The Dissolution of the Elements."
5.4. Causing revulsion toward saṃsāra:
All that is conditioned is thus impermanent, due to the scorching heat from the crest of the fire of impermanence.
"Who could always be beautiful?"— thus one forms this conceptualization consisting of error regarding this [body].
Furthermore, all of this is impermanent due to its own cause.
Because of obtaining a state comparable to the flash of lightning,
if there is such mastery over this [body],
then how could that which belongs to oneself exist here now? [5.4.2]
Furthermore, everything is indeed unreliable and not worthy of trust because it is subject to change; for that which is bent down by its end is suffering even without [the presence of] pain.
Having reached that end, how could there be happiness?
Likewise, everything is momentary and devoid of stable existence by virtue of relying upon the three times.
In that regard, who in this world would have their efforts bear fruit by rushing toward even that which is not the foremost with the thought that it is the foremost?
[5.4.4] For everything that is dependently arisen is subject to disintegration.
Because its nature is to tend toward disintegration and destruction,
for whom would the thirst for union— which, when directed toward cyclic existence, has only frustration as its fruit— not be so? [5.4.5]
This entire world is further worn out because its nature is afflicted by what is called old age;
for who, even while searching, could find any essence here?
Nothing conditioned here provides any protection, for it is itself being swept away by the destructions of the flood of existence— like wood infested by woodworms. [5.4.6]
He who, with the intention of seeking protection, should rely upon this,
will merely fall down the current;
nor is there any shelter whatsoever here.
x x x x x x x x x x x | x x x x x x x x x the foolish, having entered, become afflicted by the fire of suffering. [5.4.8]
In this world, there is no other refuge whatsoever that those afflicted by fear might resort to,
for from it only fear itself arises manifestly.
How could that very thing be the escape from it?

It is sufficient to quickly extinguish [the fire] from that very place— the abode of saṃsāra, which is agitated by the serpents of all defects and where the eye of the intellect is shrouded by the darkness of delusion.

What wise man would, through the habit of neglect, fall under the power of the sleep of trust in this world— which is mired in the mire of unexpected suffering and downfall, where action is joined solely with renunciation— yet which displays its own form as auspicious, even though it is the abode of manifold calamities? [5.4.10] And that which displays its own form as auspicious...
In this dense forest of worldly existence, which is like a treacherous enemy, what conscious person would place their trust?

To swiftly detach oneself from it for the sake of attaining well-being is sufficient for those of most skillful intellect; however, when experiencing various sufferings, it is not right to offer further entreaties to remain here. [5.4.11]
The fourth rest, titled "The Terror of Saṃsāra."
And the fifth chapter: the section on the state of dissolution.
6. The Section on Diverse Meanings 6.1. The Nature of the State of Conventional Reality: Now, this world is thus empty.
The void that remains all around, which is the locus of the elements,
will become either a defiled mind enveloped by the extreme darkness of ignorance, or it will become pure darkness. [6.1.1]
In this manner, he shall remain for twenty eons as the one who delights the people with his incomparable birth,
bearing the heavy burden of the world until the end of the aeon.
Having ascended, he has departed as if into sleep.
[6.1.2] The measure of the worlds has been studied through eons; yet whatever the extent of an eon may be, that very method is what must be explained.
For the Buddha’s word, when revealed, possesses a splendor just like the orb of the moon. Here, the city is made of iron and measures one *gavyūti* in extent.
Having fashioned [the effigy] through the artisan’s work of conceptualization,
one should cut off its head using mustard seeds empowered by the cultivation of one’s own intellect. [6.1.4]
If, then, a wise person were to remove one mustard seed from this heap at the end of every hundred years,
the heap of mustard seeds would eventually be exhausted in this manner.
But one should not proceed for even a single intermediate kalpa. Likewise, another primary city, complete with its crest, should be joined as a measure of one *yojana*.
Because that supreme sheath likewise perishes,
the great aeon goes to destruction like the ocean.
At the end of the period of its formation and duration, that king of aeons consists of eighty aeons.

"Having turned the world around once, like a single revolution of a wheel, he will depart. Beyond this, that very same rule of wandering applies; therefore, all that is yet to be and all that has been is equal—the entire mass of events occurring in the wheel of saṃsāra according to the principle already stated."

Therefore, it is not fitting for wise people to plunge into this ocean— which is a realm of manifold fears and resembles the whirlpools of a river— but rather they ought to reach its shore, which provides refuge from all dangers.
This concludes the first rest-period, titled "The States of Being Enveloped," in the sixth section.
6.2. The Method of the Two Dissolutions:
When the time for dissolution arrives, people sometimes grow weary of all the objects of sensual pleasure, even those accompanied by joy.
Then, having prepared the third dhyāna as his provisions for the journey,
he proceeds to the realm called Śubhakṛtsna, which is the summit of the Saṃvarta fire.
This entire world of the physical basis, devoid of sentient beings, [is consumed].
As if arising from the pain of separation, seven moons appear;
through that perception, as the water increases on all sides, he enters it with his whole being and goes to destruction.
Furthermore, at another time, when all people had perished,
he understood that sensual pleasures— though accompanied by pleasure— are corrupted by many defects; thus,
he relied upon the fourth dhyāna, which is conducive to tranquility.
The wind rises and, having reached the realm called Bṛhatphala at the summit of the world-system,
blows fiercely and incessantly all around, destroying this receptacle-world.
Even the earth, fire, water, and treasures, when shaken,
seek refuge in destruction rather than in safety;
for the abode known as Sahā, along with all its sentient beings, is consumed by the threefold dissolution.

Just as all this [world] inevitably approaches a threefold fall into destruction, so too do other elements (*dhātu*), which are the abodes of infinite beings, go to ruin; therefore, that which is conditioned is not permanent—this is the true teaching of the Sage. [6.2.5]
In the sixth book, the second rest, titled "The Method of the Two Cycles."

6.3. Because he explains that the world has its cause in karma and other such factors, the Conqueror of Enemies reveals the true meaning [of reality]: that it has no creator-god as its cause, that it is not linear [in time], and that it does not exist prior [to its arising].
By teaching the doctrines of non-causality, the cause of liberation, eternal existence, and the beginninglessness of the world, he rendered the teachings of the wicked sectarians insubstantial;
he declared that destruction occurs through the power of fire, water, and wind.
Then he set aside those doctrines concerning the future limit;
for does not this sun, having dispelled the preceding darkness, drive away the subsequent mass of gloom as well? [6.3.2]
Demonstrating the diverse purposeful activity— such as burning, moistening, and shaking— that pertains to all worlds,
the Lord of the Gaṇas refuted the doctrine of non-existence among the followers of the Gaṇas.
[6.3.3] A vessel containing no more than a handful of water is devoid of essence.

Through its destruction, there is suffering; through the non-arising of this [suffering], there is the cause [of liberation]; and through the application of the method for its opposite, there is the path to liberation.
Demonstrating the means for the abandonment of all that is to be discarded by every philosophical system, the All-Seeing One revealed the stage of tranquility,
which arises from the disillusionment with conditioned phenomena and is designated as "cultivation. [6.3.4]

He spoke to the earth so that the world’s transgressions might be eliminated by his prowess; yet the earth did not say, "No," for passion does not perish. Thus, even that earth was taught the method of the instruction on dispassion, according to which one becomes no longer subject to training (*aśaikṣa*). [6.3.5]

Having heard these words of the Sage— peaceful, profoundly tranquil, and intended for a purpose other than worldly gain— the disciples, being fully capable of attaining peace, shall lead themselves to the excellent, higher state, which is threefold and conforms to their own nature.
It is not at all surprising that this conduct is so virtuous, for the world of the righteous is indeed a world beyond darkness.
With the mind fixed upon the primary source of the elements, it proceeds toward all particular manifestations.
This concludes the third rest, titled "The Illumination of the Meaning of Being," in the sixth section.
At the conclusion of the narrative, the entire earth, together with its mountains and subterranean realms, trembled; all the arts and sciences were shaken.
With scattered flowers as its ornaments, it shone with a resonant humming; suddenly, by the thousands, the gods rejoiced,
while the great host of Asuras was thrown into agitation.
By the Lord who always bears that which is ever-shining,
who is without sound, and who desires the welfare of the virtuous,
the sky— resplendent with the manifestation of the world— has been conquered. [6.4.2]
Together with people who subsist on the nectar of hope for dense rain-clouds, and with those who slowly feed only upon the wind,
even the thick clouds driven by the breeze pass away.
The auspicious light of the Sun was swiftly brought forth.
Indeed, no enmity transcended its course; in that even step, the newly assembled gods and demons met together.
Bringing that charming manner which made even the assembly of Indra shine,
the Lord also revealed a discourse free from doubt.
Having provided for the welfare and happiness of men, he shone forth,
surrounded by his hosts who were free from physical ailments, like the sun with its rays that dispel the calamity of darkness. [6.4.5]
Then, illuminating the further Dharma and leading the three worlds to the supreme state that is the abode of discipline,
he caused his own doctrine— honored by the wise— to flourish.
Having awakened and perceived that his extensive duty as a Sugata was accomplished,
he— by the power of his radiance— rendered the earth, including its serpents, humans, gods, and asuras, brilliantly luminous.
Like the moon with its full circle of digits, the Tathāgata,
having established himself in equanimity, has attained peace. Then,
as if out of extreme grief, she became unsteady and trembled.
Like a bride without a husband, the earth— its essence now dense with grief,
its crest of forest flowers trembling— shook the people who were already vessels of sorrow. [6.4.8]
Having shaken off the spray of tears scattered throughout the world, the wind, which had brought about a state of subjugation like that of scattered pearls,
adorned the earth with those very drops.
Adorned in many ways for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others,
the hosts of serpent-kings, with the jewels of their hoods as ornaments,
rise up on all sides, themselves becoming the very decoration.
The inhabitants of the ten worlds, having assembled, caused the ocean— filled with many jewels and mingled with their own tears— to overflow in manifold ways. [6.4.10]
Overwhelmed with grief, the inhabitants of Kusumapura bore away the body of the sage on various kinds of litters accompanied by the resounding noise of many musical instruments. [6.4.11]

The All-pervading Lord, out of compassion, attained enlightenment in order to bring about the beautiful and enduring welfare of men; by that very compassion, which had been long accumulated, his body was now presided over.
When the Sage, who was as tranquil as the setting sun, had departed from the sight of men, his teaching assumed a terrifying aspect through the various forms of the constituent elements. [6.4.12]
With loud roars, they rose up to overwhelm him, like untimely clouds;
yet, having encountered them as adversaries, he remained unharmed. [6.4.13]
The assembly of the Lord of Munis, the elephant that destroys impurity and free from passion,
having directed the quarters with the teachings consisting of the recited liturgy, performed the command of the Victor through exceedingly radiant sounds.
Being proclaimed in many ways by virtuous people who have determined the meaning attained by the compilers of the scriptures, and who have discarded evil doctrines through wisdom and compassion;
This narrative has been composed by me out of a desire for the welfare of the world. Whatever in this is well-spoken shall belong to the Buddha;
and if there is anything that is redundant, that is mine.
The sun alone provides light;
its darkness does not rob the power of sight.
This is so regarding these words of the Buddha through the method of the practice of cultivation.
By whatever merit, auspicious through its purity, has been acquired by me— by that, having personally understood all phenomena,
may I show them to humanity as if they were held in the palm of my hand. [6.4.17]
Thus ends the final rest, titled "The Succession of Gurus."
And the sixth [section], the Chapter on Diverse Subjects.
And the narrative of the Great Destruction is completed.
The work of the great poet, the venerable teacher Śrī Bhadanta Sarvarakṣita.
The verses amount to three hundred and ninety; when calculated according to the *anuṣṭubh* meter, they measure five hundred and thirty-four. (Gra Pra 534)
